48230.title: Introduction to Engineering Projects
48230.description:
This core subject exposes you to ideas regarding the scope of what engineering actually is, considerations regarding engineering in the Australian context, and the broad impacts engineering decisions have on people, community and the environment. Through authentic engineering experiences you will build your professional skills and knowledge, providing a solid foundation for your continuous professional development journey as a future engineer.

The subject is centred around completing the Engineers Without Borders Challenge for which you will work in a team to develop engineering solutions to local real-world challenges on behalf of a partner Australian Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander Community Organisation. You will form a team with peers and working together in and outside class you will research and refine the problem and design considerations, ideate and prototype potential solutions that will work in the community context, and ultimately propose a fully developed design idea that would benefit the partner community.

In completing the challenge you will develop your professional interdisciplinary skills such as research skills, learn and apply the engineering design process, develop an understanding of and consider socio-technical issues, build your professional communications skills in engineering contexts, and learn to lead and participate in team processes.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an awareness of Indigenous Australian cultural, historic, and contemporary contexts in order to inform work in a complex project. (A.1)
Identify user needs to inform the development of a design solution. (B. 1)
Apply a design thinking approach, using appropriate engineering techniques and tools, to develop a solution that meets user needs. (C.1)
Communicate a design solution clearly and concisely to stakeholders using appropriate format and presentation. (E.1)
Explain the collaboration and contributions of team planning, communication and problem-solving in developing a design solution. (E.1)

48430.title: Fundamentals of C Programming
48430.description: In this subject, you will focus on the C programming language and will learn how to collect, process, and store data. You will explore essential programming concepts like conditional statements, loops, functions, arrays, file handling, data structures, and managing memory with pointers. You will also learn how to compile C code, link files, and run your programs using the GNU toolchain. You will experience the full development cycle just like an embedded/low-level system programmer, from analysing complex problems to designing, coding, debugging, and testing your solutions in C. This hands-on approach ensures you gain practical skills and confidence in programming.
learningOutcomes: Design, develop and test programs in C programming language to solve problems related to collecting, processing and storing data. (C.1)
Identify and explain the use and workings of programming tools (such as compilers, linkers and debuggers), standard libraries and operating system functions to support program execution. (D.1)
Demonstrate the understanding and the ability to follow professional programming practices to align with industry expectations. (D.1)
Communicate effectively and collaborate as a team member to solve complex problems using C programming language. (E.1)

48433.title: Software Architecture
48433.description: This subject covers essential concepts, methodologies, and practical skills for designing, developing, and assessing software architectures. You will gain hands-on experience with architectural tools, techniques, and real-world scenarios. This subject prepares you to tackle complex software architecture challenges and make informed architectural decisions in your professional career. You will apply the industry practices to architect a business system, ensuring it aligns with professional standards.
learningOutcomes: Describe the factors that affect the architectural context and requirements, including stakeholders and their interests, architectural qualities, business requirements and usage scenarios. (B.1)
Develop and refine multiple views of a software system architecture, based on the conceptual, execution and implementation architecture. (D.1)
Understand the key issues in choosing and implementing architectural patterns, including performance, testing, security, usability, maintainability and reliability qualities. (D.1)
Reason about alternative architectural designs to satisfy a system's quality attributes. (C.1)
Develop a complete software architecture for a proposed solution to a realistic industry problem. (C.1)
48433.recommended:
It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have knowledge of object-oriented design and unified modelling language (UML) – this can be demonstrated through completion of any of the prerequisite subjects or the Foundations of Programming: Object-Oriented Design course available on lynda.com through the UTS: Library.

A quiz is provided to check mastery of the expected prerequisite knowledge. Students are advised to attempt this quiz in the first few weeks of the session.

48436.title: Digital Forensics
48436.description: In this practice-based subject, you will engage in laboratory-based learning to determine if a crime has been committed through the acquisition, analysis, and reporting of digital evidence. Your studies will focus on forensic analysis of network data, including the recovery of website visitation evidence relevant for court cases, alongside scrutinising digital storage devices to identify and retrieve critical data. You will also delve into the examination of operating systems to unearth hidden data, perform detailed analysis of metadata to gain deeper insights, and apply rigorous forensic principles to produce sound and defensible reports. Through these hands-on activities, you will develop a comprehensive understanding of digital forensics and its applications in real-world scenarios.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate theories of digital forensics. (D.1)
Understand the structure of forensic evidence. (D.1)
Implement forensically sound digital security practices in industry. (B.1, C.1)
Demonstrate competence in applying industry-standard forensic analysis techniques. (D.1)
48436.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject be confident with using Windows command line utilities such as netstat, nslookup, net and ipconfig; Linux command line tools such as grep, ls, uname and ps.

48730.title: Cybersecurity
48730.description: This subject equips you with vital cybersecurity skills, addressing the dual aspects of people management and technology to mitigate risks like legal repercussions, financial losses, and eroded trust. You'll develop a robust understanding of cyber-attacks, defense mechanisms, and security services—confidentiality, integrity, availability. You'll also gain hands-on experience with industry-standard technologies such as IPSec, SSL, PGP, and S/MIME. Through practical application, you'll be prepared to enhance the cybersecurity posture of contemporary organisations.
learningOutcomes: Recognise and compare major theories and principles that are used in the implementation of a secure network. (D.1)
Apply the underlying algorithms used to construct Security Protocols. (D.1)
Identify and recognise major security threats and their mitigation strategy. (D.1)
Explain major methodologies for secure networks and what threat they address. (D.1)

Applied examples, laboratory work, and workshops are key components, reinforcing theory with practical skills.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply fundamental concepts and technical terms of materials science and engineering.
Describe the mechanical and physical behaviour of materials and evaluate the impact of standards on material performance.
Solve materials selection problems and critically assess selection procedures.
Apply various chemistry terms, molar calculations and chemical equations appropriately.
Prepare a professional consultancy report evaluating mechanical properties of materials.

65111.title: Chemistry 1
65111.description: Chemistry is central to understanding the world around us and it provides foundational knowledge for many other scientific disciplines such as medicine, biochemistry, energy and technology. This subject will provide you with fundamental knowledge and skills in chemistry. Through the lectures you will learn about atomic theory, structure and bonding, chemical reactions and equilibria, quantitative chemistry, molecular geometry, and intermolecular forces. Through the practical program you will develop key scientific skills such as laboratory techniques, teamwork, observation, measurement, analysis, and problem-solving.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply key chemistry principles.
Qualitatively monitor chemical reactions and explain observations with chemical equations.
Apply quantitative skills to solve chemistry problems.
Demonstrate proficiency in laboratory techniques and practice.
Effectively communicate chemical knowledge and the significance of chemistry and its applications to diverse audiences.

65325.title: Digital Trace and Identity
65325.description: This subject introduces students to the underlying principles and applications of digital forensic science. You’ll learn about the development and expansion of the role of digital forensic science and its importance to the future of criminal investigations. The course will enhance your knowledge of the digital traces you leave behind in your own life and how these traces can be used to assist in the investigation of crime and understanding criminal phenomena. You’ll develop your practical digital investigation skills through the use of computer laboratory classes using industry standard software.
learningOutcomes: Explain the importance of digital traces to modern forensic science and evaluate their value in the investigative process
Apply forensic science principles to digital traces and investigations
Recognise and apply the appropriate tools to identify, acquire and analyse digital traces for investigative purposes
Communicate complex findings from investigations and generate an expert witness report

65326.title: Digital and Cyber Crime
65326.description: This subject examines digital and cyber crime through the identification, analysis and interpretation of digital traces. Building on prior learning in digital trace and identity and digital forensics, you will explore how digitally mediated activities generate traces across a broad and distributed digital sphere of investigation. The subject considers selected forms of digital and cyber crime, with emphasis on the investigative value, limitations and uncertainty associated with online, device-based, multimedia and other digital traces. Through asynchronous learning activities and computer laboratory classes, you will develop foundational capabilities in working with digital traces and communicating findings in digital and cyber crime contexts.
learningOutcomes: Discuss key forms of digital and cyber crime and the digital traces associated with these activities.
Characterise the digital sphere of investigation and identify relevant sources of digital traces.
Extract and analyse information from digital traces in selected digital and cyber crime case contexts.
Integrate heterogeneous digital traces to reconstruct activities, assess links and evaluate uncertainty.
Synthesise and communicate investigative findings through written, visual and/or verbal reporting formats

68037.title: Physics 1
68037.description: This foundational subject introduces you to calculus-based physics, covering mechanics (kinetics, dynamics and rotational), thermodynamics, electricity, fluid dynamics and waves. You'll learn measurement techniques, uncertainty analysis, and technical communication. The course aims to deepen your understanding of physical principles and their application in predictive modelling for engineered systems, while recognising model limitations through testing and analysis. Emphasising quantitative problem-solving using calculus and algebra, it provides a framework for modelling natural phenomena relevant to engineering design and analysis. You'll understand how physics both enables and constrains engineering, requiring compliance with physical laws and often demanding new insights or innovative model applications. The subject also offers a glimpse into the professional discipline of physics, developing analytical and observational skills, and technical communication, which are essential for innovation and will be further developed in advanced subjects. ical understanding and new physics plays a key role. This subject initiates the insights and attitudes relevant to this goal.
learningOutcomes: Solve fundamental physics problems based on understanding of the conceptual basis in mechanics, thermal physics, oscillations, waves, electricity and fluids.
Measure basic physical phenomena, analyse data and verify and apply mathematical models to describe and understand the natural world.
Demonstrate technical communication, project planning, team and time management skills.
Demonstrate understanding of the nature of physics as a professional discipline of great importance to engineering innovation.
68037.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have either completed 35010 Foundation Mathematics or are enrolled in or have completed 33130 Mathematical Modelling 1.

68038.title: Advanced Mathematics and Physics
68038.description: Delivered by the School of Mathematics and Physical Sciences, this subject equips second-year engineering and science undergraduates with the essential mathematical and physical knowledge needed in their fields. It offers a comprehensive set of mathematical tools for analysing electric and magnetic fields, circuits, and signal processing, alongside theoretical and applied quantum physics. The physics component introduces quantum physics, bridging from classical mechanics to its applications in semiconductor devices. Mathematics topics include vector calculus, complex variable functions, Divergence and Stokes theorems, Cauchy-Riemann equations, the Residue theorem, and Laplace transforms.
learningOutcomes: Solve core mathematical problems required in the engineering discipline;
Solve problems in applied and quantum physics using a range of mathematical and practical techniques;
Evaluate how the quantum properties of electrons in solids can be used to develop new electronic devices;
Interpret how the quantum and physical properties of materials have relevance to the practice of engineers and applied scientists.

68201.title: Physics 2
68201.description: This foundational subject prepares you for advanced studies by covering electrostatics, circuits, magnetism, electromagnetism, induction, waves, physical optics, and introductory atomic physics and quantum theory. It integrates current research from the School of Mathematics and Physical Sciences at UTS, linking theory to real-world scientific inquiry.
learningOutcomes: Recognise fundamental physics principles and laws and apply them strategically to a range of problems in the physical sciences.
Communicate scientific information effectively and access information from a variety of sources.
Design and evaluate laboratory experiments and analyse experimental data appropriately.
Develop individual and collaborative professional skills including accurate documentation of work.
Develop and apply appropriate physical and mathematical strategies for problem solving and data analysis.
68201.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have completed HSC Mathematics Extension 1 or 2, 33130 Mathematics 1 or 35010 Foundation Mathematics (or equivalent).

68413.title: Quantum Physics
68413.description: Expanding on waves and classical mechanics, this subject investigates the distinct behaviour of the atomic world compared to the macroscopic world we experience daily. You will learn the conceptual and mathematical basis of quantum mechanics, including quantum state vectors and operations. Using this knowledge, you will explore key phenomena in quantum physics, such as bound states, quantum tunnelling, and entanglement. The subject culminates with applications to quantum technologies, focusing particularly on qubits and quantum computation. This subject provides you with fundamental material for understanding many areas of physics and chemistry, as well as contemporary applications relevant to nanotechnologists.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate how quantum-mechanical systems, states and observables are represented by mathematical entities and analyse the measurement process and the time-evolution of states.
Solve the Schrödinger equation for common one-dimensional situations e.g. the quantum well, the tunnel barrier and the harmonic oscillator.
Apply the most common quantum-mechanical operators, especially the Hamiltonian, the position, momentum, angular momentum and the ladder operators.
Calculate and apply the stationary states and energies of the unperturbed hydrogen atom.
Apply core principles of quantum mechanics to analyse the physical basis of quantum computing, including the behaviour of qubits and basic quantum operations.

68416.title: Computational Methods
68416.description: This subject introduces the theory and practice of numerical and computational methods for solving mathematical and physical problems. You will study key techniques including optimisation, numerical integration and Monte Carlo methods, matrix methods, and the numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations, with an emphasis on practical implementation in Python. These methods are applied to modelling and simulating complex physical systems through project work, with applications drawn from areas such as quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and molecular dynamics. You will develop skills in computational modelling, data analysis, visualisation, and professional communication of results.
learningOutcomes: Describe the main algorithms for solving a range of important problems in maths, physics, and related areas
Design and implement code to solve a range of problems numerically
Explain why various numerical algorithms work, and what their limitations are

70102.title: Foundations of Law
70102.description:
This subject explores the origins of the Australian legal system and examines how its present operation is informed by its historical and cultural contexts. You will examine key ideas that underpin legal institutions, including democracy, sovereignty, the rule of law, and the separation of powers. Using several critical legal perspectives, you will also examine how the law impacts on different social groups, including those that have been historically marginalised from society’s power structures.

 The subject introduces you to the primary sources of law – judicial decisions and statutes - and you will develop key skills in analysing judge-made law and in statutory interpretation.

 Your learning in this subject will be informed by diverse academic literature, case studies, group work, student-lead discussion, and skills-based instruction on legal research. Together, the research skills and critical legal thinking taught in this subject will build a foundation for the successful completion of later subjects in your law degree.
learningOutcomes: Explain foundational legal concepts and their historical and cultural contexts.
Analyse the classification and resolution of disputes within legal frameworks and broader societal contexts.
Apply critical thinking in legal analysis to evaluate different perspectives on a variety of contemporary legal issues.
Conduct comprehensive legal research using and evaluating a variety of primary and secondary sources and methodologies.
Demonstrate integrated legal skills to independently address legal questions.

70103.title: Ethics Law and Justice
70103.description:
This subject explores the critical role that legal ethics play in shaping the profession and the broader justice system. You will examine barriers to accessing justice while also considering the reforms underway to eradicate such barriers. You'll gain insights into the conduct rules and responsibilities that govern legal practitioners and how these might be applied to members of the profession, as well as the frameworks to help you integrate ethical considerations into your decision-making processes.

Learning in this subject is dynamic and interactive. You'll engage in a series of collaborative activities, including regular small group discussion-based seminars. Through workshops on legal writing skills and peer review writing exercises, you will also focus on developing the legal writing skills you’ll need in the legal profession.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on, develop and articulate their principles of justice and response to the commitment and achievement of justice.
Recognise ethical issues and discuss the relationship between personal and professional attitudes, values and approaches to decision making, developing their own ethical framework.
Plan and complete a variety of critical legal writing tasks using academic styles, structures and expression, supported by accurate referencing.
Respond appropriately in group discussions, identifying different roles within the group dynamic and practising active listening; developing strategies and skills to collaborate effectively.
Analyse, plan, monitor and reflect upon their own performance, identifying appropriate resources and utilising feedback to improve self-management skills and to develop self-awareness and resilience.

70106.title: Principles of Public International Law
70106.description:
This subject explores the foundational principles of Public International Law. Public International Law is a well-established yet rapidly developing branch of law that seeks to respond to complex global challenges. It has a wide scope of application and far-reaching implications for States, individuals and other actors including corporations and civil society. Public International Law is increasingly relevant for all areas of legal practice and for understanding Australia’s position in the world.     
 
The topics you will examine in this subject are the key building blocks of Public International Law: the nature and scope of the international legal system, sources of international law and its relationship with national law, legal personality and recognition of states and governments, jurisdiction and immunity from jurisdiction, law of treaties, state responsibility, and settlement of disputes and use of force under the United Nations Charter. 
  
In this advanced-level subject, you will collaborate with classmates to analyse case studies and solve scenario-based problems addressing contemporary issues in Public International Law. You will work on a small-group project to develop your collaborative and communication skills.
learningOutcomes: Understand how the international legal system regulates the behaviour of nation States through the formation of international rights and obligations.
Apply rules and principles of international law to matters of contemporary international concern.
Critically evaluate the rules of international law and formulate legal arguments based in treaty and custom, synthesising judicial decisions, scholarship and soft law.
Effectively collaborate with peers to convey legal ideas, and inform, analyse, and persuade.
Develop logical, reasoned and persuasive oral legal arguments, managing competing time and task demands

70107.title: Principles of Company Law
70107.description: This subject critically examines the role and operation of companies registered under the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and other business structures involving trusts and associations. You will examine in detail the life cycle of the company from formation to the internal operation including directors’ and officers’ duties, members meetings and rights, through to the termination of companies in distress and external administration. Through the application of statutory interpretation, skills to real-world problem questions, you will develop a detailed of how to advise companies within the legislative and regulatory framework. You will also explore the role of state regulation of corporate activity using a range of social, political and theoretical perspectives. Through collaborative practical exercises such as tutorial discussions, and drafting legal documents, you'll develop the skills required by corporate lawyers. By participating in debates and group work, and independent analysis in your research essay task, you will refine your analytical abilities and learn to critically evaluate policy positions and the role of the modern company in Australia.
learningOutcomes: Locate, analyse and apply the principles, doctrines and structures of Australian company law to solve legal problems involving the rights and liabilities of members, creditors and officers of Australian companies;
Draw on theoretical and practical knowledge and independent research in to order to critically evaluate the adequacy of Australia’s current framework of corporate law and the scope for reforms;
Apply and justify professional ethical judgment to address complex issues relating to the impact of diversity, cultural and gender values in corporate law settings;

Creatively and analytically evaluate facts, problems and issues raised in a range of corporate law disputes and respond with effective arguments that critically appraise the available options for parties involved.

70110.title: Introduction to Law
70110.description:
The subject is designed to provide students from a range of disciplines and backgrounds with a fundamental understanding of the Australian legal system, the Common Law traditions underpinning it and its operation within the Australian federal structure and the Westminster system. Its objective is for students to develop an understanding of the Australian legal framework and the role of law and then consider the law in a business context in regulating individual and commercial relationships. This provides a basis for undertaking further studies in law in Australia.

An overall introduction to the subject is provided in the ‘Get Started’ Module. The subject topics are then structured in eleven Modules numbered 1-11. The Modules comprise topics which address learning about the Australian legal system and the civil, criminal and business relationships it regulates, and several topics covering public international law. Modules 1-3 introduce students to the Australian legal system and help them understand the operation of Australian law. These topics aim to equip students with a foundational understanding of the operation of the Australian legal system to enable an effective transition into the more specialised learning involved with Modules 4-9. Modules 10-11 explore international law with some reflection on the relationship of Australian law to international law. Module 12 enables students to revise the main topics for exam preparation.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of the law and the Australian legal system including its Common Law traditions along with historical, sociological, jurisprudential, cultural, ethical, philosophical and international contexts;
Critically analyse fact scenarios to identify legal issues and solutions;
Apply legal principles to fact scenarios and discussion questions to evaluate the likely legal outcomes for client advice or legal controversies; and
Succinctly summarise a key case to reflect its core principles, outcomes and implications for future cases of a similar kind and subject matter.

70211.title: Contracts
70211.description:
This subject deals with the formation, interpretation and termination of contracts. You will explore the requirements for a contract to be considered legally binding, the terms required for a contract to remain valid, what constitutes a breach of contract, when a party to a contract may end performance of it, and when a party’s consent to contract may be vitiated.

Through video lectures you will develop your initial understanding, which will then be developed in tutorials. By collaboratively working on problem questions, you will practice your problem-solving skills, including critical analysis and evaluation, to apply legal principles to various scenarios. You will use these skills to provide a written advice, thereby developing your written communication skills.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a coherent understanding of the fundamental elements of contract law, using appropriate legal authority and citation;
Building on the matters covered in 70103 Ethics Law & Justice, understand ethical challenges arising in key areas of contract law;
Critically analyse fact scenarios to identify contractual issues;
Identify and apply relevant contract law to fact scenarios and evaluate the likely legal outcomes in order to advise a party of their contractual rights;
Apply legal problem-solving skills to produce a clear, rational, coherent and professional written response to a contract law question using appropriate legal authority and citation.

70311.title: Torts
70311.description: This subject examines the law of torts, which deals with claims for civil wrongs. You’ll explore aspects of torts such as trespass to the person, trespass to land, negligence and nuisance, with a particular focus on the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW). Torts is a topic required for admission as a legal practitioner in all Australian jurisdictions and provides you with foundational knowledge required for more advanced subjects in the law degree. Learning takes place in collaborative, discussion-based classes where you’ll focus on the key cases and statutes in detail. Each week you will collaboratively engage in solving set problems that enable you to apply your readings to factual scenarios. By the end of this subject, you’ll be equipped to analyse complex problems, including causes of action and possible defences, and advise each party on their rights and liabilities.
learningOutcomes: Apply selected key concepts of the common law of torts and the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW) with reference to the basis of liability, forms of action and interests protected in the law of torts, and the adaptability of Tort law to societal changes.

Critically analyse the policy, development and application of the law of torts, making reasoned choices amongst alternatives to develop logical, justifiable and structured arguments, and advice to parties as to the tortious rights and liabilities in specific scenarios.

Recognise the perspectives of various stakeholders in selected tort cases and the role of a professional lawyer in advising on claims in Tort law, including evaluation of how lawyers’ ethical duties to clients and courts are addressed with respect to negligence.

Apply cases, statute law and secondary sources to generate appropriate written and oral responses to questions of individual rights and liabilities in Tort law, as well as to issues of legal policy and theory.

Initiate and complete self-directed learning through engagement with legal materials to prepare for class-based discussion and problem solving; and to complete assessment tasks with attention to due dates and required criteria.

70327.title: Introduction to Property and Commercial Law
70327.description:
In this subject students explore the rights and obligations of persons engaged in commercial transactions involving personal property. The main topics include rights arising from dealing with personal property generally; the sale of personal property; consumer protection and the provision of finance secured by personal property.
You will examine what is meant by personal property and how legal rights arise depending on the nature of property being dealt with as well as the type of transaction.
While the focus is on personal property and legal rights you will also be introduced to concepts of trusts and equitable interests and aspects of real property. This coverage is an introduction to the subsequent core subjects 70517 Equity and Trusts and 70317 Real Property.
You will gain the relevant legal knowledge from readings, podcasts and vodcasts. You will also develop skills in statutory interpretation as much of the subject involves dealing with major legislation.
The application of legal concepts and legislation will be put into practice in weekly seminars. These seminars will enable you to develop skills in critical legal analysis as well as statutory interpretation.
Students are expected to have completed the listed readings and to have engaged with the online materials prior to each class. Further, students within each tutorial group will be assigned set tasks at the commencement of the session in which they will be required to lead class discussion on directed issues. This responsibility is non-assessable but is a useful motivation for a students to immerse themselves in a topic for a week.
Your assessment will include the weekly quizzes, a practice-oriented file note exercise and a final exam.
By engaging with the material and participating in tutorials, you will build a solid foundation in dealing with personal property in the context of commercial law transactions as well as developing an expertise in reading statutes. These skills will prepare you for more specialised subjects and ultimately professional legal practice.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply the law relating to commercial transactions with a particular focus on personal property transactions and related concepts of finance law.
Apply statutory interpretation skills to navigate, interpret and apply specific legislation to solve legal problems.
Critically analyse how the law may affect common commercial transactions and make reasoned choices amongst alternatives.
Develop a logical and justifiable argument as to how legislation affects common commercial transactions involving personal property.

Accurately assess their capabilities, wellbeing and performance by undertaking and initiating self-directed work and learning, including identifying gaps in their own knowledge and skills and determine how best to eliminate those gaps.

70417.title: Corporate Law
70417.description:
This subject provides you with a comprehensive overview of the key principles of Australian corporate law under the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth). You will examine issues such as the formation of Australian corporations, corporate decision-making processes and corporate governance, and the role of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission in regulating companies, financial markets and financial services. You’ll also develop your appreciation of the involvement of indigenous peoples with Australian corporations. 

You’ll develop your skills in applying the relevant principles of Australian corporate law to hypothetical problems in interactive tutorials. Through collaborative practice-based exercises, you will practice tasks that corporate lawyers are commonly involved in - including simulated meetings and the provision of advice to clients.  You will also reflect on the adequacy of Australia’s current framework of corporate law in balancing the interests of various stakeholders, as well as the scope for reforms.
learningOutcomes: Correctly apply the relevant legal rules to communicate well-reasoned advice to internal and external stakeholders of Australian companies about their rights and liabilities;
Critically evaluate the adequacy of Australia’s current framework of corporate law in balancing the interests of various stakeholders and the scope for reforms;
Appreciate the competing ethical, social responsibility and commercial factors that may impact upon the business of Australian companies, and formulate strategies for managing potential conflicts;

Understand the role of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission in regulating Australian companies, financial markets and financial services to ensure honesty, integrity and accountability;

Demonstrate the capacity to be a reflective and resilient professional who can implement appropriate self-management and self-directed learning strategies to address gaps in their current knowledge and skills.

70616.title: Australian Constitutional Law
70616.description: This subject equips you with a solid grasp of Australian Constitutional law, focusing on the Commonwealth Constitution's role in our legal system. You'll gain insights into federalism and the fundamentals of State constitutional law, the power distribution between the Commonwealth and States, and the interplay of Commonwealth legislative, executive, and judicial powers. You'll also examine the express and implied rights and freedoms within the Australian Constitution. Through analysis of constitutional texts, cases and High Court interpretative approaches, you'll develop the ability to research, solve, and forecast constitutional issues. This is essential, as Constitutional law underpins the Australian legal system and is a prerequisite for legal practice. Your learning journey includes practical exercises to enhance your understanding and application of Constitutional law.
learningOutcomes: Explain the philosophies and principles that shape Australian Constitutional law, the content of the Commonwealth Constitution, the fundamentals of state constitutions and the role of the High Court in interpreting the Commonwealth Constitution.

Locate, evaluate and organise information from recognised sources, using their research to generate a written legal argument that synthesises legal and contextual principles and issues, in order to critically evaluate and address Constitutional issues.
Prepare logical, succinct and persuasive responses to constitutional problems that are supported by relevant evidence and appropriate for a professional legal context.
Examine a set of facts, identify relevant Constitutional issues raised and consider Constitutional principles and cases, to determine the likely success of arguments for or against constitutionality.

Critically engage with the relationship between First Nations people, the Australian Constitution and legal institutions, including the Federal Parliament, High Court and Executive branch of Government.

76023.title: Deceptive Trade Practices and Product Liability
76023.description:
This subject examines the statutory actions in the Australian Consumer Law (ACL). Because the remedies under the ACL are usually easier to establish than remedies available at common law or in equity, legal practitioners often rely on the statutory action of misleading and deceptive conduct as an alternative to traditional claims.

You will examine how loss or damage is assessed, as well as the connection between a contravention of the ACL and any loss or damage suffered. You’ll also explore the remedies available under the ACL. Learning will involve case study analysis, participating in seminar discussions and conducting research for a case note.

You will also develop your presentation and communication skills through presenting a seminar paper in class in group formatt simulating presentations you would give in a work environment. This presentation will be then presented as a written report. Final assessment will focus on topical issues that are affecting consumers and businesses alike in this area of law. The aim is to develop practical skills needed to work with clients, understanding of statute and applicable case law which is changing rapidly.

In the ACL we will focus on misleading and deceptive conduct (S18) but will further explore misleading representations, product recalls, manufacturer’s liability and statutory guarantees, all of which are tools to provide protection for consumers, businesses and society in general. We will focus on the remit of the ACCC and their operations and priorities.

We will further focus on the role of the Courts and its interaction with the ACCC in implementing and enforcing the ACL. This subject is well suited to all consumers. From a career perspective completing this subject will stand you in good stead for working in the area of competition and consumer law in law firms, working with the ACCC, working as in house legal counsel in businesses or even working in a non legal capacity in businesses providing services to consumers.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of Australian Deceptive Trade Practices and Product Liability laws.
Critically evaluate the Australian Consumer Law remedies and how they are applied.
Critically evaluate the concept of ‘norm of conduct’ demanded by the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 in commercial dealings.
Demonstrate advanced research and communication skills and generate accurate and persuasive legal arguments.

76027.title: Competition Law
76027.description:
This subject provides you with a comprehensive and engaging examination of the economic and legal principles of competition law (also known as antitrust law or restrictive trade practices law) in Australia. You will explore key aspects of statute law, particularly Pt IV of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (CCA), and how common law courts interpret the CCA. You will also understand how the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) operates and policy issues.

The course covers the evolution and objectives of Australian competition law and how it is administered and enforced both nationally and internationally. You will gain in-depth knowledge of major anti-competitive statutory conduct in Part IV of the CCA, including civil and criminal cartels, anti-competitive agreements (including concerted practices), secondary boycott, misuse of market power, exclusionary dealings, resale price maintenance and mergers and acquisitions. You will learn about the administration and enforcement of competition law in Australia.This includes authorisation and notification regimes, remedies for private litigants, and other related matters.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse the rationale for, and implementation of, competition policy and law in enhancing market efficiency in both a static and ongoing sense, and to adjust quickly to the needs of law firms with competition practices
Effectively and persuasively communicate critical analysis of a variety of major issues on competition law and policy;
Interpret and explain the practical operation and enforcement of competition law in business and commerce;
Analyse and evaluate selected business scenarios in relation to international enforcement of competition law, in which Australia is involved.

You will examine insolvency within the social context as well as the impact of insolvency law. You’ll also explore the legal procedures involved in insolvency law, as well as the impact of insolvency on stakeholders such as employees, creditors and debtors. Both individual and corporate insolvency are examined. 

You will learn through weekly readings and podcasts that provide a framework for understanding foundational concepts. You will then class join small and large group discussions to further explore the main issues. Each week you will also analyse a hypothetical problem scenario that will simulate a legal advice session where you’ll advise the client of their legal position and offer advice that is legally sound and commercially appropriate for the client’s situation.

Critically assess and synthesise the range of commercial and legal issues that arise during times of financial difficulty;
Efficiently and effectively identify and apply electronic and paper-based research strategies to inform and facilitate the formulation of sound oral and written legal arguments for clients;
Effectively balance and synthesise the competing interests of different stakeholders involved in an insolvent estate.

79032.title: Competition and Consumer Law
79032.description:
This subject offers you a comprehensive and engaging exploration of competition law (antitrust law) and consumer law (deceptive trade practices law) in Australia. You’ll understand why these laws are crucial, what they entail, and how they are enforced. You’ll learn the importance of competition and consumer laws in ensuring fair markets and protecting consumers. By understanding these principles, you can critically assess current legal frameworks and their impact on the economy and society.
You’ll delve into the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (CCA), its evolution from the Trade Practices Act 1974 (TPA), and its interpretation by common law courts. You’ll also explore major international treaties on antitrust and consumer law enforcement involving Australia. Current issues and recent cases will provide you with real-world context.
The subject is structured into three parts for better clarity and focus. First, you will trace the evolution of competition law in Australia, understand key legislative features of the CCA, examine major anti-competitive conduct (including monopolistic agreements, misuse of market power, and mergers/acquisitions), and learn about enforcement mechanisms such as authorization and notification regimes and available remedies.
Next, you will grasp the policy objectives of consumer law, study general prohibitions under Schedule 2 of the CCA - the Australian Consumer Law (ACL) (such as misleading or deceptive conduct, unconscionable conduct, and unfair contract terms), and explore enforcement issues to understand how consumer rights are protected. Finally, you will analyse major international treaties on consumer protection and competition enforcement, and review significant international cases involving Australia to understand global implications.
By the end of this subject, you will have a strong understanding of the economic and legal principles that underpin competition and consumer laws in Australia. You’ll be equipped to critically analyse and engage with these laws, both in a national and international context, preparing you for a career in law, policy-making, or business.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the rationale for, and implementation of, competition and consumer policy and laws in enhancing market efficiency and promoting competition and consumer welfare.
Analyse and apply competition and consumer law principles to legal problems in a commercial context to achieve legitimate business objectives for clients.
Demonstrate critical analysis and written communication skills to generate accurate and persuasive legal arguments.

81529.title: Futuring for Innovation with Impact
81529.description: In this subject, you will think beyond the world as it stands today and consider the different futures that may impact your personal innovation practice towards sustainability. You will learn critical research skills and futuring methods to identify trends that shape future worlds. You will explore your own innovative area of interest and assess how possible futures may impact or inform your innovation. This futuring process will leverage qualitative data to identify barriers and enablers to change, to support the design your innovations to have an impact and make a difference towards sustainable development. This subject is hands-on and will broaden your horizon.
learningOutcomes: Analyse real-world innovation contexts and cases in order to discern connections and patterns that are supportive of emergence of ideas, innovation and change.
Identify issues of interest or concern, and apply a range of disciplinary and professional practice approaches to examine the potential for action.
Analyse trends observed in real-world contexts and creatively combine futuring methods to speculate about future developments.
Apply appropriate methods to conduct enquiry into real-world challenges to identify their constitutive elements and connections situated in specific contexts.
Evaluate the alternatives and articulate a compelling argument for a proposed direction for innovation in response to a real-world challenge.

81538.title: Frame Innovation
81538.description: This subject centres on frame creation, a design-based approach to networked problem solving, developed and used in the UTS Design Innovation Research Centre. Working with the multidisciplinary staff from the centre, participants in this subject engage with the question of how to 'solve the unsolvable' – the open, complex, dynamic and networked problems facing society today. Participants learn the theory behind the nine-step frame creation methodology, putting into practice and testing its associated methods and tools. Through first-hand experience of the power of frame creation, participants create new approaches to problems that have confounded conventional problem-solving practices. They then shift towards the broader practices of frame innovation – the skills, knowledge and mentality required to drive frame creation in an organisation and society.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and apply techniques for understanding, visualising, interpreting and investigating diverse problems.
Collaborate effectively in team-based decision-making.
Evaluate and communicate the effectiveness of creative problem-solving methods.
Explore and ideate using the Frame Creation methodology.
Use a range of media and techniques creatively and critically to develop ideas, strategies and practices in response to a client brief.

81539.title: Innovation in Complex Systems
81539.description: The challenges that we face today have become increasingly complex and connected. 91123.title: Nature and Evolution
91123.description: The existence of all species on Earth today has been made possible through the evolution of a vast diversity of biota. This subject explores the considerable variation among living organisms and how they interact with their environment, addressing the question what enables life to exist in the range of habitats across the globe. You’ll examine the adaptations that bacteria, archaea, protists, plants, animals and fungi have evolved over time in response to changing environmental conditions and that allow biota to inhabit the vast array of ecosystems on Earth. The major taxa are explored with reference to  their evolution over time, that is movement from water to land and in some cases back again. You’ll conduct a short-term monitoring experiment to explore the important biotic and abiotic requirements for a sustainable ecosystem, generate testable hypotheses, collect scientific data and communicate the research findings. The subject concludes with a reflection of today’s pressures on biodiversity and how these shape current trends in evolution and species diversity.
learningOutcomes: Explain the fundamental principles of evolution by natural selection and its role in shaping the diversity of life on Earth.
Evaluate the role of environmental factors in driving evolutionary processes and shaping species distributions.
Distinguish among the major groups of organisms within each biological kingdom using key adaptations over evolutionary history.
Design and test a hypothesis about ecosystem function, collect data and interpret experimental findings.
Communicate effectively about evolutionary biology topics through scientific discussions, written syntheses and oral presentations.

Interactions with key stakeholders will help you build professional networks, equipping you with practical skills to leverage these networks for initiating change.
learningOutcomes: Collaborate to explain and visualise entrepreneurial ecosystems.
Identify elements and gaps in the entrepreneurial ecosystem and envision levers to influence the ecosystem.
Responsibly engage with others in the entrepreneurial ecosystem with a view to develop longer-term professional relationships.
Develop a proposal to launch within the ecosystem, and a strategy for it to enhance the system.
Evaluate the impact that your proposed initiative within the ecosystem might have from practical as well as ethical considerations.

Through this, students test their emerging expertise, learn to collaborate across differences, and develop insights that have the potential to create new pathways for real-world action.

95007.title: TD: Pathways to societal transitions
95007.description:
For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives."

Artificial Intelligence seems to be everywhere – embedded in phones, homes, workplaces – but what are the physical infrastructures that make it possible, and how are they reshaping communities and our environment? This subject takes students beyond the screen to investigate the hidden, material side of AI. From data centres and fibre-optic cables to the vast demands for energy, water, and land, students will explore how rapidly expanding digital infrastructure is transforming communities and environments globally, and in their own backyard.

Students will hear from a diversity of industry experts working across sectors who are making digital infrastructure expansion possible, and learn how the challenges and opportunities this expansion presents affect sustainability efforts globally, and in Australia. In multidisciplinary teams, students will investigate how digital infrastructure expansion is unfolding in their local community and codesign future scenarios that balance environmental priorities with societal demand for AI. Through this process, they will use a range of ethnographic and creative research methods, including photography, video, and story-making, to learn from their local community and communicate possible futures. This process will be assisted through regular engagements with our industry partner, Lane Cove Council, who will provide first-hand insights into how digital infrastructure expansion is shaping their community.

Students participating in this subject will develop skills and confidence in understanding and responding to complex, real-world challenges in multidisciplinary teams, using effective systems approaches to change-making. It is relevant to students from all disciplines including (but not limited to) computer and data science, social sciences, fine arts, communications, science, law and medicine.
learningOutcomes: Integrate different perspectives to unpack and analyse complex challenges that the digital infrastructure industry is creating for local communities and environments.
Identify significant issues and emerging opportunities to create positive change in real-world contexts.
Apply transdisciplinary and creative research methods and collaboration in teams to generate responses to complex challenges.
Develop a cohesive rationale for proposals and communicate ideas persuasively to diverse audiences.
Synthesise your learning and research to generate insights about transdisciplinarity and your own role in imagining digital futures, and steps to bring about positive social change.

How can we transform ourselves and the systems we live in? This subject invites students to explore the deep connection between personal transformation and systemic change. Through embodied, reflective, and collaborative learning, students engage with practices from mindfulness, complexity science, implementation science, decolonial thinking, and First Nations and other diverse knowledge systems. Across two integrated phases—self-transformation and systems evolution—students learn to sit with the discomfort of change within complex systems, understand the roots of suffering and injustice, and take ethical action in response to real-world challenges co-designed with our industry partner Stockland. Through creative, non-written assessments, students map their inner shifts, design micro-interventions within complex systems, and showcase ripple effects of their work through ritual, installation, and action pledges. Learning flows between immersive in-person sessions, interactive online sessions, and reflective practices, supporting students to build purposeful, relational, and sustainable approaches to social impact within the communities they care about.

95728.title: Health Statistics
95728.description:
Understanding and using data correctly is crucial for planning and decision-making in public health. By taking this subject, you will gain the essential knowledge and skills needed to analyse and interpret health data, and critically evaluate the results of epidemiological studies. This subject will teach you key statistical concepts and tests used in public health. In this subject, you will focus on learning how to interpret statistical outputs and use the right analysis methods, rather than computing or programming skills. By the end of the subject, you will know how to select appropriate statistical analyses based on research questions and study designs. The skills and knowledge you gain will be directly applicable to real-world scenarios.

This subject uses a blended learning approach, combining online and on-campus activities. You will learn the theoretical aspects of health statistics through online lectures and materials. These online resources will also include activities to deepen your understanding and help you prepare for on-campus tutorials. During on-campus tutorials, you will apply what you have learned by using statistical software, giving you hands-on experience. An activity book will guide you throughout the subject. Expect to spend about 10–12 hours per week on all learning activities, including self-directed learning, on-campus sessions, and completing assessments.
learningOutcomes:
Construct and explain research questions to enable responsible and ethical decision making and research in
public health.
Compare and contrast different types of statistical analysis.
Perform and interpret basic statistical analyses using a statistical software package.
Communicate the results of statistical analyses

97101.description:
This subject is designed to provide students who have no prior knowledge of the Chinese language with basic reading, listening, speaking and writing skills. You'll learn Pinyin for pronunciation and acquire your vocabulary by around 200 words. Through active participation in collaborative activities, you'll develop intercultural competence, learning to navigate between cultures.

Your learning will involve a communicative approach, engaging in interactive tasks and activities to enhance language proficiency. You will be expected to prepare for classes through various exercises and utilise online and peer resources. The language learning approach will focus on linguistic and cultural practices across the Chinese world.

You'll be expected to commit to approximately 12 hours of weekly study, including class time, and immerse yourself in Chinese both inside and outside the classroom to build confidence and fluency.
learningOutcomes: Comprehend and respond to basic texts in oral and written Chinese.
Produce basic texts in oral and written Chinese.
Demonstrate intercultural awareness across two or more cultural contexts.

99218.title: Intercultural Communication
99218.description: This subject provides an introduction to the core concepts and debates in the interdisciplinary field of intercultural communication. It is designed to help prepare students for the interpersonal and dynamic nature of working in increasingly globalised workplaces and intercultural environments. Using a problem-based approach, students learn to critically examine numerous frameworks and theories to interpret intercultural encounters in praxis-based scenarios. The applicability of specific strategies and approaches in intercultural communication are also examined for their relevance to industry, communities and in society more broadly.
learningOutcomes: Critically engage with intercultural communication theories and frameworks and apply these theories to analyse diverse cultural situations and spaces
Reflect on own perceptions of intercultural spaces and encounters and intercultural skills development for professional and everyday contexts
Design and conduct independent, ethical, small scale research about aspects of interculturality
Recognise the ongoing impact of colonialism on and positive contributions of Indigenous cultures in intercultural spaces
Communicate effectively and appropriately in written and oral academic English

976111.title: Contemporary China
976111.description: This subject provides an overview of contemporary China and its history, culture, politics, society and economy. You will learn to identify and analyse current issues from multiple perspectives using theory and methods for intercultural research. The subject combines lectures with tutorials and independent work to develop your analytical and problem-solving abilities in China studies, with a focus on cultural diversity, social and economic change, and political transformation. You will learn to develop comparative and ethical approaches for critical thinking and verbal and written communication skills, reflecting the subject's multidisciplinary approach. Topics include cities, gender, home and work, identity, governance, media, the economy and China's international relationships.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on and analyse contemporary China in its historical, political, cultural, social, and economic dimensions.
Employ approaches and frameworks to engage in historical, political, cultural, social and economic inquiry.
Apply knowledges of China ethically in their reflective and inquiry-based works.
Demonstrate critical problem-solving and research-led analytical skills in the context of China.
Communicate effectively in English the findings of independent inquiries and reflections in written form.
Maintain good academic practice, observing ethics and referencing standards.

976211.title: Contemporary Japan
976211.description: This subject provides an overview of contemporary Japan, examining its history, politics, culture, society, and economy. You'll acquire critical skills to pinpoint and analyse current issues, using theoretical and methodological frameworks for intercultural research. The subject combines lectures with independent work to enhance your problem-solving and analytical abilities in Japan studies, with a focus on cultural diversity, social change, and ethical practices. You'll develop critical thinking and communication skills, reflecting the subject's multidisciplinary nature. Early topics cover foundational concepts of Japan Studies, while subsequent weeks delve into Japanese identity, politics, work life, gender and Japan's international relationships.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on and analyse contemporary Japan in its historical, political, cultural, social, and economic dimensions.
Employ approaches and frameworks to engage in historical, political, cultural, social and economic inquiry.
Apply knowledges of Japan ethically in their reflective and inquiry-based works.
Demonstrate critical problem-solving and research-led analytical skills in the context of Japan.
Communicate effectively in English the findings of independent inquiries and reflections in written form.
Maintain good academic practice, observing ethics and referencing standards.

976411.title: Contemporary France
976411.description: This subject blends lectures and independent and collaborative learning to provide a foundational understanding of contemporary French society, politics and culture. You'll develop critical thinking and intercultural research skills. In weeks 2 and 12 you'll follow an umbrella programme shared by all European contemporary society subjects, exploring identity, divisions and crises in Europe. Between weeks 3 and 11 you'll explore France's historical evolution and the concept of French identity, with special focus on France's 'revolutionary' spirit, the importance of its Republican values, and its relations with former French colonies. These elements are crucial for understanding France's place in the modern world and the social and political issues shaping contemporary French society.

976421.title: Contemporary Germany
976421.description: This subject blends lectures, independent and collaborative learning to provide a foundational understanding of contemporary German history, politics, society, and culture. You'll develop critical thinking and intercultural research skills, essential for advanced In-country Studies. In weeks 2 and 12 you'll follow an umbrella program shared by all contemporary European society subjects, exploring its identity, divisions, and crises. Between weeks 3 and 11, you'll focus on Germany's post-World War II era, examining its divided past, reunification, and current challenges, including identity, social movements, economic growth, immigration, and international relations, alongside language issues and popular culture. These elements are crucial for understanding Germany's place in the modern world. German popular culture is dealt with throughout.

976451.title: Contemporary Spain
976451.description: This subject introduces you to contemporary Spain through its historical, political, cultural, social, and economic dimensions from a local, national, continental, and global context. You will be provided with the critical skills to identify, reflect, and analyse major current socio-cultural challenges that shape contemporary Spain through the learning of theoretical and methodological approaches for engaging you in intercultural research. In weeks 2 and 12, you will follow an umbrella program shared by all contemporary European society subjects that introduces general issues relating to contemporary Europe: definitions, geographical space, addressing its identity, unification, internal divisions, colonialism, and the impact of migration, among others. In the other weeks, the subject focuses on divergent and historical ways of conceptualising Spain. You will learn about important moments in Spain’s history, such as the unification, the Second Republic, the Civil War, the Franco dictatorship, the restoration of democracy, and the sociopolitical developments of recent decades. You will delve into the diversity of national and cultural identities (regionalisms), plurilingualism, gender, film, music, art, migration, economics, and the evolving socio-cultural aspects of contemporary Spain. This subject will also provide you with an understanding of some of the current challenges that the country faces and how a Spanish citizen thinks and feels in the twenty-first century. The collaborative and reflective learning activities will allow you to develop your intercultural capabilities via critical thinking on Spain's diverse and dynamic culture(s), as well as an international perspective. In the assessments, you will apply your critical and reflection skills to identify and analyse contemporary Spain, through theoretical and methodological approaches.

Maintain good academic practice, observing ethics and referencing standards.
